25.1.intro: One stolen password can cost more than a bad month. Thieves love ad accounts because they can spend your money fast. One hour of lock-down closes most doors.

steps.say: List every account the business needs: email and domain, Shopify, Meta, Google, TikTok, your email tool, payment providers, bank, and domain registrar.
steps.check: You have one list of every account.
steps.lost: Write down your 5 most important accounts.

steps.say: Turn on two-factor login (a second check after your password) on each. Use an authenticator app or security key, not text messages.
steps.check: Every account asks for a second check at login.
steps.careful: Text message codes can be stolen by moving your number to another SIM.
steps.lost: Turn on two-factor for your email first.

steps.say: Keep a different long password for every account in a password manager.
steps.check: No password is used twice.

steps.say: Save each account's backup codes offline, where a trusted person can reach them.
steps.check: You can get back in if you lose your phone.

steps.say: Make at least 2 trusted people full admins on Meta, Google and Shopify, each with their own login.
steps.check: No one shares a login, and no single person can lock you out.
steps.lost: Add one trusted admin on Meta.

steps.say:
Every quarter, tidy who has access.

1. Remove people who no longer work with you.
2. Look over admin and partner lists for anyone you don't know.
steps.check: The access check is on your Helix calendar.

steps.say: Turn on login and spending alerts by email and phone.
steps.check: You hear about strange activity within minutes.
steps.careful: Report cybercrime in some countries at ReportCyber (cyber.gov.au) and in the US at the FBI's IC3 (ic3.gov).
steps.lost: Turn on login alerts for Meta.

25.2.intro: Meta keeps your ad accounts, Pages, pixel and people in a business portfolio. Whoever owns it controls everything, so it must be you.

steps.say: Make the business portfolio yourself, with your business email. Make yourself and one trusted person admins.
steps.check: You own the portfolio and have a backup admin.

steps.say: Do business verification when Meta asks. Use your legal name, address and documents exactly as registered.
steps.check: The portfolio shows as verified. Missing a deadline can pause ads.
steps.lost: Use your name exactly as registered.

steps.say: Make the ad account inside your own portfolio. Give agencies and freelancers partner access only.
steps.check: The ad account lists your portfolio as owner.

steps.say: Set an account spending limit a little above your planned monthly spend.
steps.check: A thief can't spend more than the cap.

steps.say: Add a backup payment method.
steps.check: A failed card doesn't restrict the account.

steps.say: Check billing currency and time zone before your first ad.
steps.check: Both are right. They can't be changed later without a new ad account.
steps.careful: Outside the US: if GST registered, add your ABN in Meta billing so you're not charged GST, and check your card's international fee. US: use a business card, and call the card company before raising budgets.

steps.say: Connect the ad account to Helix.
steps.check: Helix pulls your Meta spend and results each day.

25.3.intro: Ad accounts get restricted for failed payments, policy flags, identity checks or odd activity. Most can be fixed if you stay calm and follow Meta's process.

steps.say: Open **Account Quality** in Meta. Read the exact reason.
steps.check: You know why the account is restricted.

steps.say: If a payment failed, fix the payment method and pay any balance owed.
steps.check: Billing shows nothing owing.

steps.say: If Meta asks for identity checks (photo ID or video selfie), do them in the official app or Help Centre only.
steps.check: The check is sent through an official channel.
steps.careful: Meta never asks for passwords or payment by direct message. Ignore fake "Meta support" messages.

steps.say: Request a review once, with a short, factual explanation. Then wait.
steps.check: One review request is in progress.
steps.lost: Ask for one review. Then wait.

steps.say: Don't open new ad accounts or portfolios to get around it.
steps.check: You avoid looking like you're dodging the rules.

steps.say: While you wait, keep sales coming from email, Google and free posts.
steps.check: Sales keep going while ads are paused.
steps.lost: Send one email to your list.

steps.say: Afterwards, write down the cause and fix it: backup payment, policy-safe ad words, landing pages that match the ad.
steps.check: The same problem is unlikely to happen again.
steps.lost: Write the cause in one line.

25.4.intro: Speed matters. A hacked ad account can spend thousands in hours. Do these steps in order.

steps.say: Turn off every active campaign you didn't make. Then pause all campaigns.
steps.check: Nothing is spending.

steps.say: Remove unknown people and partners from your business portfolio and ad account.
steps.check: Only people you know have access.

steps.say: Change your passwords (email first, then Meta). Sign out of all sessions.
steps.check: The intruder is logged out.

steps.say: Call your bank. Block the card linked to the ad account and ask about disputing the fake charges.
steps.check: No more money can leave, and a dispute is started.

steps.say: Report the hack at facebook.com/hacked.
steps.check: Meta has a case open.

steps.say: Write a timeline with screenshots: when you noticed, what was spent, what you changed.
steps.check: You have proof for Meta, the bank and police.

steps.say: Report the crime (see Lesson 25.1). Keep the reference number.
steps.check: You have a reference for your bank and Meta.

steps.say: Once safe, add the protections in Lessons 25.1 and 25.2, especially a spending limit.
steps.check: The account is locked down.
steps.careful: If someone set up a fake store or ad in your name, tell customers and report the fake pages to Meta.

25.5.intro: An agency can save time. But your accounts, data and history must stay yours.

steps.say: Before you sign, list what you must own: ad accounts, pixel and datasets, Shopify, domain, email tool and Google Ads. Give the agency partner or user access only.
steps.check: Every account is owned by you.
steps.lost: Check you own your ad account.

steps.say: Put in the contract: you own all accounts, content and data, plus the notice period, handover steps and the reports you get.
steps.check: The contract says you own everything.
steps.careful: Say no to contracts that say the agency owns the ad account.
steps.lost: Add one line: I own all accounts and data.

steps.say: Ask for a monthly report showing spend, sales, profit and what they changed.
steps.check: You understand every report.
steps.lost: Ask for spend, sales and profit each month.

steps.say: To leave, give notice. Ask for a handover pack: campaign notes, audiences, creative files and any logins they set up.
steps.check: You have everything to run ads yourself.

steps.say:
On the last day, close everything off.

1. Remove their access from every account.
2. Change any shared passwords.
3. Check billing so nothing still charges their card.
steps.check: The agency has no access.

steps.say: If the agency owns your ad account, ask in writing for a transfer. Or make a new account in your portfolio and share your pixel to it.
steps.check: You run ads from an account you own. Old campaign history may stay behind, but pixel data is yours.
steps.lost: Ask in writing for the account.

steps.say: For your first month alone, change one thing at a time. Watch profit daily in Helix.
steps.check: You see what each change does.

steps.say: Check ad accounts, ads, customer lists and reports are in your name (Meta **Business Settings > Ad accounts**, Google **Admin > Access**).
steps.check: You own every account and asset.

steps.say: Ask your agency to report MER (all ad spend as a share of all sales) and contribution profit, not just ROAS (sales for each $1 of ads).
steps.check: Agency reports show profit numbers.

steps.say: If you bring work in-house, start with the daily ad check (Lesson 7.6). Keep specialists for the gaps.
steps.check: You run the daily check yourself.
steps.lost: Do the daily ad check today.

25.6.intro: Phone networks and inboxes now check that messages really come from you. Unregistered senders get labelled or sent to spam.

steps.say: In your email tool's settings, set up SPF, DKIM and DMARC for your sending domain (three records that prove email is really from you).
steps.check: The tool shows the domain as authenticated.
steps.lost: Follow your email tool's domain guide.

steps.say: Send from your own domain, never a free email address.
steps.check: Emails come from you@yourbrand.
steps.lost: Use your brand email as sender.

steps.say: Register your text sender details with your SMS provider before sending campaigns.
steps.check: Texts show your business name, not "Unverified".
steps.careful: Outside the US: since 1 July 2026, business name senders must be on the national SMS Sender ID Register, matching your business name, trademark or domain. US: standard numbers need carrier registration (10DLC), and toll-free numbers need verification.
steps.lost: Ask your SMS provider how to register.

steps.say: Use the same sender name everywhere.
steps.check: Customers recognise you in every inbox.
